pages.x: In 1804, after renegade Ottoman soldiers murdered dozens of Serbian village leaders, the survivors met at Orašac and chose a pig trader, Karađorđe, Black George, to lead a rising. It grew into a war for freedom. Crushed in 1813, it flared again in 1815, and by 1830 Serbia ruled itself as a princedom inside the empire.

Greek merchants abroad had formed a secret society, the Friendly Society, to free Greece. In March 1821 risings broke out in the Peloponnese, and within months the rebels held much of the south. Both sides killed civilians: when the Greeks took Tripolitsa that autumn, thousands of its Muslims and Jews were massacred.

Laskarina Bouboulina, a twice-widowed ship owner from the island of Spetses, spent her fortune on the revolution. She commanded her own ships in the blockade of Nafplio and rode into Tripolitsa when it fell. Greeks remember her as a heroine of the war; she was shot dead in a family feud in 1825.

In 1822 an Ottoman force landed on the rich island of Chios, which had been drawn into the revolt. Tens of thousands of Greeks were killed, and tens of thousands more were sold as slaves. Eugène Delacroix painted the horror in a huge canvas that turned many Europeans toward the Greek cause.

Europe's educated classes had grown up on ancient Greek books, and many saw the war as the land of democracy rising again. The English poet Lord Byron spent a fortune on Greek forces and went to fight himself, but caught a fever at Missolonghi and died there in April 1824, aged 36. Greeks still honour him.

With the rebels fighting among themselves, the sultan called on Muhammad Ali, the powerful governor of Egypt. In 1825 his son Ibrahim landed in the Peloponnese with a modern army and began to win it back. Missolonghi fell in 1826 after a year's siege, when its starving people tried to break out by night and most were cut down.

Britain, France and Russia decided to force a truce. In October 1827 their fleets sailed into the bay of Navarino, where the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet lay at anchor. A shot was fired, and a battle nobody had ordered began. In four hours most of the Ottoman ships were sunk or burned. It was the last great battle of wooden sailing ships.

After losing another war to Russia, the sultan gave way. In 1830 the powers declared Greece independent, and in 1832 they gave it a king: Otto, a 17-year-old Bavarian prince. The new state was small and left most Greeks outside it, and the dream of gathering them in drove its wars for the next century.

Serbia and Greece were the first nations to win their freedom from the Ottoman Empire, and the other peoples of the Balkans followed over the next hundred years. Greece also showed how public feeling in Europe, stirred up by poets and painters, could pull great powers into a faraway war.
